newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bourse banking on technology to add value.
newsitem.headline: German bourse banking on technology to add value.

text.p: Germany's stock exchange is banking on using technology to add value rather than merely competing on price, according to one of the top executives of the stock exchange holding company.

"Cost has a very important role to play, of course, but if one can provide a quick transparent system providing more information, then people will pay an extra pfennig or whatever," Joerg Franke, management board member of Deutsche Boerse AG told a reception late on Thursday.
Speaking at the Frankfurt International Business Journalists' Forum, Franke said there would be further automisation of trading procedures in key products such as the heavily-traded Bund futures.
He also said that at the beginning of May the bourse plans to launch a product based on spreads between long-term government Bunds and the more medium-term Bobl bonds.
This type of product was only possible using electronic trading systems, Franke said.
"People are turning around as they realise electronic trade is cheaper. Also, a fast market is very important and speed is improving as technology improves."
Franke also said that trading in the Schatz future, a futures contract on debt with remaining maturity of 1.75 to 2.25 years, will begin on the DTB German futures exchange on Friday.
The moves come as Franke forecast further consolidation among small European bourses in coming years but with larger bourses remaining independent in the run-up to European monetary union.

As to the impact of the single currency, due to be launched in 1999, Franke said it was still too early to forecast how it will affect trading and in what denomination different products will be traded.
"Little will happen until the middle of next year, after that we will have a better idea," Franke said.
He also said there was strong competition between the different European government bonds. "We think the mark will be the benchmark but then the French, for example, think differently," Franke said.
Unity in the debt market would be difficult to achieve as there were differences between states in terms of liquidity, credit rating, and taxation.
Franke confirmed that co-operation talks with the French exchange Matif had finished. "It hasn't worked out and we have ceased discussions for the moment," he said.
